I am 58 years old and have been farming in Quzhou County for over 30 years. Unlike some of my neighbors, I finished high school, so I pay close attention to what the county extension station recommends. I know our land on the North China Plain is good, but it is also overworked, so I try to manage inputs carefully. 

This year, I will stick to the wheat–maize rotation that has always fed my family and provided steady income. I have eight mu of good irrigated land. The winter wheat is already in the ground from last October; it is coming out of dormancy now, so my immediate job is to top-dress it and irrigate at jointing. After the wheat comes off in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid summer maize using no-tillage seeding to catch the remaining moisture and save time. I use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed because the yield advantage is obvious, and I save my own wheat seed only if I cannot get fresh certified seed. 

For fertilizer, I used to apply too much nitrogen like everyone else, but after attending extension meetings I now use compound fertilizer more precisely. I apply basal compound before wheat sowing and top-dress with urea at green-up. For maize, I apply compound at seeding and side-dress urea at the big-flare stage. Phosphorus and potassium come entirely from the compound bags; I do not buy straight phosphate or potash because our soil still carries some residual phosphorus from years of heavy application, though I maintain moderate levels to be safe. 

Irrigation is from my tube-well. Wheat needs four critical irrigations: overwintering, jointing, heading, and grain-filling. Maize needs two: one at jointing/tasseling and one at grain-filling if the summer drought sets in. For crop protection, wheat gets a pre-emergence herbicide, an insecticide at jointing, and a fungicide at heading; maize gets a post-emergence herbicide and two insecticide sprays during the summer. I use rotary tillage before wheat sowing to break the maize stubble, but maize is planted no-till directly into the wheat stubble—this preserves soil moisture and reduces costs.
